studies.title: Full When Taking, Short When Giving
studies.meaning: The offence is defined by its asymmetry rather than by its size. These are people who take their measure in full and hand it over short, and the Arabic marks the difference with two verbs: one for exacting everything owed, one for causing a loss. Nothing is said about how much is skimmed, because the amount is not the point. Then the argument turns without warning to the resurrection, as though a question about scales were the same question as a question about standing before God.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan by the reckoning the surah is usually given, though some early reports place it at the very beginning of the Medinan period and connect it with the markets there. The commentators record the difference rather than settling it. Either way the audience are traders. Measuring by volume and weighing by stone were the two mechanisms by which almost every transaction in the region was completed, and both were operated by the seller.

keyTerms.note: From a word for the small amount at the very edge of a vessel. The name identifies the offence as taking the rim rather than the sack, which is why it can be done constantly without ever feeling like theft.

A form meaning to demand complete payment of what is due. It is not a criticism on its own; the same root gives the word for fulfilling a promise, and the fault lies entirely in the contrast that follows.
A causative from the verb to lose, so the seller is described as making the other party lose rather than as gaining. Arabic puts the emphasis on the damage done rather than on the profit taken.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Grain was sold by a measure the seller owned, and dates and oil by weight against stones he kept himself. There was no standards office. A merchant with a slightly generous measure for buying and a slightly shallow one for selling could operate for years, and everyone knew such measures existed without being able to prove which ones they were. The whole market rested on a trust nobody could verify.
studies.didYouKnow: The word the surah is named after occurs once in the Quran, and it comes from a term for the tiny amount that sits at the very brim of a container. The offence is named by the smallest quantity in the language, not by the act of cheating, so the chapter's title is essentially the word for a rim.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage joins two things that usually sit far apart, market practice and the resurrection, and it makes the second the answer to the first. What is presumed missing in a short-measurer is not honesty but expectation: he does not think he will be stood up and asked. That places belief in the last day at the root of ordinary commercial conduct rather than in a separate compartment of religion.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same two acts together, full measure and an accurate balance, and calls the result better in outcome.
Raises the balance alongside the sky, so weighing rightly is set inside the order of creation itself.
Shows an earlier prophet sent to a prosperous people with this exact charge about measure and weight.

studies.applyIt: Find the place where you give slightly less than you take, and it is unlikely to involve scales. The hour you bill, the effort you put into a favour returned, the attention you give a conversation you started. Pick one and level it up today, quietly. Nobody will notice, which is the closest you can get to the situation this surah describes.

studies.title: The Record Called Sijjin
studies.meaning: Standing is the first thing described about that day, and the word for it suggests waiting rather than trial. Then the surah names where the record of the unrestrained is kept, using a term it immediately admits the reader cannot know. The question is asked and the answer given is not a location but a description of the document: a book inscribed. Scholars differ over whether the name is a place, a prison, or the register itself, and the sources hold the readings side by side without deciding.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah moves from a market offence to the reckoning in four lines, and the commentators treat the whole middle section as an expansion of the question asked in the fourth ayah, whether such people expect to be raised. No occasion is reported. The image of a written register would have been immediately intelligible to a mercantile audience, whose disputes were settled by producing documents.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form usually linked to the root for imprisonment. The classical readings take it as a place beneath the earth, a register, or a name given without explanation, and the commentaries record all three.
From a verb about writing in distinct marks or numbers, used of a document whose entries cannot be confused. It implies a record already completed rather than one still being compiled.

The plain verb for standing, with no object. It describes people on their feet before the Lord of the worlds, and the commentators note that waiting on your feet, not the verdict, is what the ayah chooses to show.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A commercial dispute in a trading town ended with someone producing a document. Debts, deposits and shares in a caravan were written down, witnessed and kept, and the strength of a claim was the strength of its paperwork. A man who had cheated by a rim's worth over twenty years had left no single entry anyone could point to, which is exactly the situation this passage answers with a book already written.
studies.didYouKnow: The line describing the record here is repeated word for word eleven ayat later, where it describes the record of the dutiful instead. The same three words serve both destinations. The two names given to the registers, however, occur nowhere else in the Quran, so this surah is the only place either word appears.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers a question about knowledge by admitting the limits of it. It names something, asks how the reader could possibly know what it is, and then gives only what can be given: it is written. That method appears repeatedly in the Quran and it does two things at once, refusing to let the term be domesticated into a picture and insisting on the one fact that matters, which is that the record exists.

crossReferences.why: Gives the matching passage for the other register, with the identical question and the identical answer.
Describes a book brought out spread open, with the reader told to read his own account.
Shows every community called to its book, and says the record speaks about them in truth.

studies.applyIt: Notice, once today, the difference between what you would say about your conduct and what a plain written entry would say. Not a moral judgement, just the entry: the time, the amount, the words used. Most people find the two versions differ, and the surah is entirely about a case where only the second one survives.

studies.title: Rust Over The Heart
studies.meaning: A woe already pronounced is now explained. Those who deny the day of reckoning are described in one clause and it is a moral description, not an intellectual one: an aggressor, sunk in wrongdoing. When the verses are read to him he has a phrase ready, and it is the phrase used across Mecca. Then the surah gives the mechanism, and it is metallurgical. What they kept earning has laid a film over their hearts. And with that they are said to be screened from their Lord.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The dismissal quoted here, that the message is old stories, is recorded in several surahs as a stock Meccan reply, which suggests a phrase in circulation rather than an individual's judgement. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The commentators connect the explanation given in the fourteenth ayah to a well-known saying preserved in the tradition about a black mark that spreads on the heart with each wrong act.

keyTerms.note: Connected with the verb for writing in lines. The dismissal is not that the message is false but that it is old material already recorded, which was the standard reply and appears repeatedly in the Quran.
Used of a film that forms on metal or of drink clouding the mind. The verb occurs once in the Quran and describes an accumulation, not a blow: the covering arrives through repetition.
A passive participle from the word for a curtain hung between two parties. It occurs once in the Quran, and the classical writers read the screening as the loss of what the other group is granted.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Iron in a coastal climate rusts fast. A sword or a blade left in a damp store for a season came out furred and dull, and the film had to be scoured back with sand and oil before the edge would take. Nobody watched it happen; it appeared. That is the exact shape of the image here, and it is drawn from a chore rather than from a philosophy.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for the covering of the heart occurs once in the whole Quran. The tradition preserves a saying that when a person commits a wrong a black mark is placed on the heart, and that if he turns back it is polished away, but if he persists the marks spread until they cover it, and this ayah is cited as the reference for that saying.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Disbelief is described here as accumulated rather than chosen, which changes what the passage is doing. Nobody decides to have a rusted heart. It comes from what was earned repeatedly, so the mechanism runs through conduct rather than through argument, and it explains why the reply to a recitation was a phrase rather than a thought. The screening at the end is stated as consequence, not as punishment.

crossReferences.why: Describes coverings placed over hearts so that they cannot grasp it, and the same dismissal quoted afterwards.
Uses a different metaphor for the same condition, a seal set on hearts and hearing, with a covering on sight.
Asks whether they do not ponder the Quran, or whether there are locks upon their hearts.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you now find easy that used to trouble you, and that you would not defend if a friend named it. That is the process this ayah describes and it is the only part of it you can observe from inside. Name it once today. Rust is scoured off with attention, and attention starts with saying what is there.

studies.title: The Other Register
studies.meaning: Two lines finish the first case: the fire, and then a sentence spoken to them naming what they used to deny. Then the surah turns, and the turn is made by repeating its own words. The same particle of refusal, the same construction, the same phrase about a record, with one noun changed. The register of the dutiful is in a place whose name means height, and the reader is again told he cannot know what it is, and again given the same three words: a book inscribed. The symmetry is exact and deliberate.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is built in matched panels, and the commentators point out that this is the hinge: everything after it answers something before it, down to the repeated phrasing. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The audience were people who had heard the first half of the surah address a specific market fault, and the second half now describes the other outcome without naming any specific virtue at all.

keyTerms.note: A verb for entering a fire and being exposed to it, used also of warming oneself at a blaze. The Arabic keeps both senses alive, and the emphatic particle before it removes any conditionality.
An intensive plural from the root for height, formed unusually. Classical readings take it as the highest reaches, a register kept there, or simply a name, and the sources record the range.
From a root joining truthfulness, kindness and the keeping of an oath. It names people by conduct toward others rather than by belief, which fits a surah that opened with a market.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Records in that world had physical locations, and the location told you the status of the document. A contract of consequence was lodged with a man of standing or kept in the sanctuary itself; a note of no importance stayed in a merchant's own box. Naming where a register is kept was therefore a statement about what kind of document it was, and everyone hearing the two names understood the contrast before they understood either word.
studies.didYouKnow: The three-word description of the record is given twice in this surah, identically, once for each destination, and it is the only thing the two registers are said to have in common. Both of the names given to their locations occur nowhere else in the Quran. The surah invents no vocabulary for the second half; it reuses the first half and changes one noun at a time.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two outcomes are described in matching grammar, which makes a quiet claim: they are the same kind of thing, recorded in the same way, differing in content rather than in nature. Nothing is said about the dutiful having done anything in particular. What separates the registers is where they are kept, and the passage's refusal to describe either place keeps the reader's attention on the record rather than the room.

crossReferences.why: Gives the matching panel for the other register, in the same words with one noun changed.
Also sorts people into matched groups and adds a third, the foremost, who are brought near.
Shows both records handed over, one in the right hand and one in the left, with the words each person says.

studies.applyIt: The surah never says what put anyone in the second register. Try the same restraint for a day: when you do something decent, do not narrate it to yourself afterwards or file it anywhere. Just let it be done. That absence of self-accounting is the nearest thing to the posture this passage describes.

studies.title: Faces You Can Read
studies.meaning: The register is witnessed by those brought near, and then the account of the dutiful begins. They are in ease, on couches, and the verb given them is simply looking. Nothing is said about what they see. Then the surah does something rare and turns to the reader in the second person: you would recognise the brightness of ease on their faces. Recognition, not description. And the first thing they are given is a drink whose seal has not yet been broken.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage answers the earlier scene of people who dismissed the message and had their hearts filmed over, and the commentators note that the sequence has moved from what cannot be seen, a register in a place with an unexplained name, to what anyone could read at a glance, a face. No occasion is reported. The vocabulary of couches, sealed vessels and perfumes belongs to the luxuries of the wealthy trading world.

keyTerms.note: A passive form, so their nearness is something done to them rather than achieved. The same word returns four ayat later, where they are the ones who drink from the spring that flavours everyone else's cup.

Used of a face that looks well and of a plant in full condition. It names a visible physical state rather than an emotion, which is why the passage says you would recognise it rather than that you would be told.
Closed with a seal that must be broken before use, the mark of a vessel nobody has touched. The same root gives the word for a seal set on hearts, used earlier of the other group.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A sealed jar was a guarantee. Wine, oil and perfume travelled by caravan in vessels closed with clay or wax and stamped, and the seal was the only proof that nothing had been drawn off or watered on the road. A merchant would pay more for an unbroken seal than for the contents. Being handed a sealed vessel meant being given something first, before anyone else had taken from it.
studies.didYouKnow: The two lines describing the dutiful reclining and looking are repeated word for word thirteen ayat later, at the very end of the surah, where they describe the believers watching the deniers. The identical ayah appears twice in one chapter with two different sets of people in view, and the second time the looking has an object.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reward is described here as visibility rather than possession. The register is witnessed, the faces are recognisable, and the drink arrives with an unbroken seal. Everything about the passage concerns what can be seen and by whom, which stands directly against the earlier statement that the other group is screened from their Lord. What is being contrasted is not comfort against pain but sight against a curtain.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for radiant faces and gives the looking its object, toward their Lord.
States the opposite condition in this same surah, a group screened off from their Lord on that day.
Also names brightness and joy on faces, and links them to what was endured with patience.

studies.applyIt: Look at the faces of three people you pass today and notice how much you read from them without deciding to. That involuntary reading is exactly what this ayah appeals to when it says you would recognise it. Then remember, briefly, that yours is being read the same way, and let that be all.

studies.title: Something Worth Competing For
studies.meaning: The seal on the drink turns out to be musk, so the last thing about the vessel is its scent rather than its contents. Then the surah interrupts its own description to say that this is what competitors should compete over, which is the only instruction in the whole chapter. The mixture is named, and those brought near drink it undiluted. And then, with no transition at all, the scene changes to a street in Mecca where believers are being laughed at as they walk past.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The mockery described in the closing section is the best attested social fact about the early community: a small group, many of them without protection, walking through a city where their new practice was treated as an entertainment. The commentators connect the passage to that period generally rather than to a single incident. No specific occasion is reported, and no individuals are named in the Quran's account.

keyTerms.note: The seal itself rather than the act of sealing. Commentators differ over whether the musk is what closes the vessel or the taste left at the end of the draught, and the sources give both readings.
From a root about a soul or a breath, so the verb carries the sense of striving for something you want badly. It is the only imperative directed at the reader in the whole surah.
A reciprocal form for exchanging signals with the eye or the eyebrow. It occurs once in the Quran and describes mockery conducted silently between two people about a third who can see them doing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Musk came overland from the east and was among the most expensive substances in Arabia, sold by tiny weights and used a grain at a time. A merchant might handle it once a year. Setting it as the stopper of a jar, rather than as the contents, describes a scale of expense the audience could price exactly, and they would have registered the extravagance before the image.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah contains only one imperative addressed to the reader, and it is not about honesty in the market, which is the chapter's opening subject. It is an instruction to compete, placed in the middle of a description of a drink. The verb chosen shares its root with the word for a soul, so the competing is named after the thing being spent on it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing the only command of the surah inside the description of a reward changes what the reward is for. It is not offered as compensation for the mockery described immediately afterwards, since the order of the passage puts the prize first and the humiliation second. What is established is that ambition itself is not the problem: the passage takes the competitive instinct of a trading city and redirects it rather than condemning it.

crossReferences.why: Issues the same call to race one another, there toward forgiveness and a garden as wide as the sky.
Tells each community to compete in good works, since God will bring them all together in the end.
Notes that messengers before were mocked, and that what they ridiculed came round on those who did it.

studies.applyIt: Name the thing you are actually competing over at the moment, honestly: money, standing, being right in a particular argument. Write the word down. Then, without changing anything today, sit with the ayah's suggestion that the competitive part of you is not the problem and the object might be. That is enough for one sitting.

studies.title: The Joke They Took Home
studies.meaning: The mockery is followed home. They went back to their households pleased with themselves, and the surah records the line they used, that these people are lost. Then one clause dismantles the whole performance: they had not been sent as keepers over anyone. The presumption behind the joke was a supervisory one, and it is simply denied. The final turn puts the same verb in the mouths of the other side, on a day when they are seated and looking, in words the surah has already used.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Ridicule was the city's first response to the new community and the cheapest one available, since it cost nothing and required no argument. The commentators describe a pattern of small public humiliations rather than organised persecution at this stage. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat, and the Quran names none of the parties involved on either side.

keyTerms.note: The verb for turning something over, used of going home. It appears twice in one short ayah, once for the journey and once for the state they arrived in, so the going and the mood are the same word.
From the root that gives the word for fruit, so the sense is of relishing something. Arabic uses it for people enjoying themselves at a gathering, which is exactly the domestic scene being described.

Those charged with watching over and preserving something. The word was used earlier in a neighbouring surah for the recording angels, so denying the role to these mockers puts them outside a job that already has holders.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A household in Mecca gathered in the evening and the day's material was shared out: who had said what, who had been made to look foolish, what the strange new group had done in the street. Entertainment was conversation. A joke that travelled well from the market to the family circle was social currency, and repeating it at home is how a passing sneer became a settled family opinion.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah gives the mockers a verb for laughing and then, four ayat later, hands the identical verb to the other side. Between the two, the line describing the dutiful on couches looking is repeated word for word from earlier in the chapter. So the closing scene is assembled almost entirely from words the surah has already used, with only the subjects exchanged.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The refutation offered is not that the mockers were wrong about the facts. It is that they had no standing to be issuing verdicts, since nobody appointed them keepers. That removes the argument from the field of who is right and places it on the question of authority, which is a much shorter conversation. The reversal that follows is then stated without gloating and without any description of what the laughter is about.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word to say the Prophet is not a keeper over them, so even he is denied the role.
Shows a group taken as a laughing-stock until they were forgotten, and the reward given for that patience.
Describes people who ridicule those who give what little they can, and says God ridicules them in return.

studies.applyIt: Think about what you brought home yesterday, in conversation, about someone who was not there. Most of us carry back one such item a day without noticing. Try going a single evening without offering any, and see what you would otherwise have said. That is the exact behaviour these three ayat describe, at exactly that scale.

studies.title: Have They Been Repaid
studies.meaning: The surah ends on a question, and the question is not addressed to anyone in particular. Have those who covered the truth been repaid for what they used to do. The verb chosen is not the ordinary one for recompense; it belongs to a root about reward and returning, the same root that gives the word for a garment and for coming back to a place. And the tense is completed: not will they be repaid, but have they been. The chapter that began with a woe closes without pronouncing one.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The final line follows a scene in which the mockery of the early community is answered by a reversal, and the commentators read the closing question as spoken over that scene rather than to the reader. No occasion is reported. The surah has moved from a market fault through two registers to a street and a household, and it ends by asking whether the accounts have balanced.

keyTerms.note: From a root about returning, which also gives the words for a garment and for a reward. The intensive passive form occurs once in the Quran, and it implies a return in kind rather than a penalty imposed.

The root means to cover or bury something, which is why it serves for both ingratitude and denial. Naming them by covering, at the end of a surah about a rusted heart, closes a figure the chapter has been building.
The plainest verb for doing anything at all, in a form for continuous past action. The surah's last word about them is not about belief or speech but about a habit of conduct kept up over time.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Settling up was a public event. When a caravan returned, shares were paid out in front of witnesses and everyone in the valley learned who had profited and who had lost, often within a day. A question asked aloud about whether a man had received what was coming to him was an ordinary question in that setting, and it always had an answer everyone present could confirm.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb closing this surah appears in this form nowhere else in the Quran, and it comes from the root that gives the ordinary Arabic word for a garment. The image behind the word is of something returned to a person and put back on them. The chapter that opened by naming a fault in weighing ends with a question about a return.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ending on a question rather than a statement leaves the reader to answer, which is a different position from being informed. The verb used makes the outcome a return of what was given rather than an addition to it, so the passage's last claim is one of exactness: nothing extra is imposed. That closes the circle with the first ayah, where the fault was precisely a failure to return what was owed.

crossReferences.why: Opens the surah with the fault this closing question answers, taking in full and giving back short.
Uses the same root for the best return and the best outcome, in a passage about wealth that vanished.
Ends another surah on the plain fact of a return followed by an accounting, with nothing added.

studies.applyIt: Answer the surah's closing question about yourself for one small thing rather than for a life: some kindness you did this month, some corner you cut. Has it come back yet. Sit with the fact that the honest answer is usually not yet, and let the sentence stay unfinished rather than resolving it.
